“Don't help me, Kavitha Masi. Just use it,” Naveen said, and held out the tablet.
“Where are the idli recipes?”
“Try finding them.”
Kavitha Masi tapped the screen twice. “There's just three little lines. Is that a menu?”
“It's the menu button.”
Cousin Pallavi peered over. “I thought that was decoration.”
Four of the five relatives around the dining table couldn't find the recipe list. Naveen said nothing and wrote in his notebook: menu unclear, 4 of 5. His hand itched to point at it.
Later he said, “Nobody's getting new photos until the menu says Recipes in words.”
Pallavi laughed. “Finally, someone tests a blog before making it pretty.”

qa.q: How many of the five relatives could not find the recipe list?
How might Naveen have felt while watching the relatives struggle?
qa.a: Nervous and a little disappointed but curious: he held back from helping even though his hand itched to point.

qa.q: What could Naveen do after fixing the menu, and why?
qa.a: Test again with a different set of people, since a fix that works for these five may still confuse others.

qa.q: How does the site look to Kavitha Masi?
qa.a: Kavitha Masi found it confusing instead of pretty, so she would want the menu to say clearly where the recipes are.

grounding: A student shows a rough recipe blog to five relatives, watches where they get lost and fixes the menu first.

When my recipe blog had just three pages, I did something that felt too early: I showed it to five relatives at Nani's house one Sunday. I'm Samir, and the blog was meant to collect our family's Konkani dishes.
I didn't explain anything. I handed my phone to each person and said, “Find the fish curry.” Then I just watched and wrote in a notebook.
Saurabh Mama went straight to About and got lost. Nani kept pressing the photo, thinking it was a button. Two of my aunts scrolled to the bottom looking for a menu that was hidden behind three little lines at the top. Only my cousin found it in under a minute.
That night I didn't add a single recipe. I put the menu as plain words across the top, made the photos open the recipe, and sent it to Saurabh Mama again. He found the curry in seconds.

qa.q: What did Samir ask each person to find?
What might Samir have felt watching Nani press the photo like a button?
qa.a: Samir was probably surprised and a little embarrassed, but also curious, since each wrong tap showed where the blog confused people.

qa.q: What other approach could have found the same problems, and would it work as well?
qa.a: Asking relatives what they thought would mostly get polite praise; watching them try a task shows real confusion, so watching works better.

qa.q: What was the first version like for Saurabh Mama?
qa.a: It was confusing: he went to About and got lost, but after the fix he found the curry in seconds.

grounding: Shows a student watching five relatives use a rough recipe blog, noting where they get lost, and fixing the menu before adding more.

Coach's notes, club family day, Saturday
Karthik brought five relatives to test his blog of the snacks his family's tea stall sells, and I watched from the next table. He gave each person one task, “find how to make the banana fritters”, and stayed silent while they tried.
His grandfather's brother, Jomon, tapped the logo three times, expecting a menu. His mother and two cousins scrolled past the recipe list because it sat below a long welcome paragraph. Only his aunt found it quickly. Karthik wrote down each stuck point and how long it took.
Afterwards he didn't open his list of new recipes. He moved the recipe list to the top, cut the welcome to two lines, and made the logo lead home. Before the session ended, Jomon tried again and found the fritters in under a minute. Next week I will suggest testing with classmates too.

qa.q: What task did Karthik give each relative?
qa.a: To find how to make the banana fritters.

qa.q: What might Karthik have felt while noting each stuck point?
qa.a: He was probably a bit deflated at first, but also focused and eager, since each stuck point showed exactly what to fix.

qa.q: What could Karthik try next to check the fix?
qa.a: Test with a few classmates who have never seen the blog, since relatives may already know how the family names its snacks.

qa.q: How was the first version for Jomon?
qa.a: For Jomon it was frustrating to tap the logo three times with nothing happening, but after the fix the fritters took under a minute.

grounding: A coach notes a student watching five relatives try his recipe blog, recording where they get stuck, and fixing navigation before adding recipes.
